result.topic_en: Euler completes his argument that for a prime 4q+1 the biquadratic (fourth-power) residues number q and the non-residues fall into three classes of q terms each, then deduces that such a prime divides a sum of two squares and suggests that every prime of the form 4q+1 is a sum of two squares.
result.transcription:
Tractatus de numerorum doctrina Cap. 12. 55
436. Remoto ergo casu, quo $xy$ est residuum, ponamus $xy$ esse non-residuum, et cum in
sex classibus omnia non-residua comprehendantur, in una earum $xy$ occurrere deberet; sive autem
ponamus $xy$ ipsi $\alpha x$, sive $\alpha x^2$, sive $\alpha x^3$, sive $\alpha y$, sive $\alpha y^2$, sive $\alpha y^3$ aequivalere, sequeretur
absurdum, dum $y$ vel esset residuum, vel in classem I, vel II non-residuorum caderet, vel etiam $x$
esset residuum, vel in classem IV, vel V caderet.
437. Cum igitur sex classes non-residuorum admitti nequeant, vel tantum tres sunt constituendae,
quod volumus, vel plures quam sex. Quod posterius eveniret, si nondum omnia quadrata non-residua
in classe II et V occurrerent. Sit ergo $zz$ non-residuum in neutra harum classium contentum, et
ex eo resultabunt tres novae classes, singulae $n$ terminis constantes:
VII. $z$, $\alpha z$, $\beta z$, etc. VIII. $z^2$, $\alpha z^2$, $\beta z^2$, etc. IX. $z^3$, $\alpha z^3$, $\beta z^3$, etc.
438. Nunc vero, ut § 435 ostendetur, neque $xy$, neque $xz$, neque $yz$ esse posse residuum, quia
inde plura residua, quam revera sunt, sequerentur. Deinde si $xy$ in quapiam sex primorum classium
contineretur, eadem incommoda orirentur, quae ante; ex quo $xy$ in quapiam trium postremarum
classium esse deberet. Videamus ergo, num $xy$ ipsi $\alpha z$ aequivalere posset.
439. At si $xy$ ipsi $\alpha z$ aequivaleret, $xz$, quia certe est non-residuum, vel ipsi $\beta y$, vel $\beta y^2$,
vel $\beta y^3$ aequivaleret; quare cum $xy - \alpha z$ et $xz - \beta y^\nu$, denotante $\nu$ vel 1, vel 2, vel 3, essent
divisibilia per $4q+1$, foret $z(xy - \alpha z) - y(xz - \beta y^\nu)$, hoc est $\beta y^{\nu+1} - \alpha z^2$ quoque divisibile,
sicque $\alpha z^2$ aequivaleret ipsi $\beta y^{\nu+1}$, ideoque in alia classe contineretur, quod aeque esset absurdum.
440. Sic igitur demonstratum est, si divisor primus fuerit $4q+1$, residua diversa biquadratorum
fore numero $= q$, neque plura, neque pauciora, non-residua autem tribus classibus comprehendi,
quarum quaelibet constet $q$ terminis.
441. Quare cum residua diversa ex biquadratis $1, 2^4, 3^4, 4^4, \ldots 16q^4$, quorum multitudo est
$= 2q$, oriantur, bina debent esse aequalia. Hinc si $a$ sit numerus quicunque minor quam $2q$,
dabitur semper alius $b$, et quidem unicus pariter non major quam $2q$, ut $b^4$ et $a^4$ aequalia relinquant
residua, seu ut $b^4 - a^4$ per $4q+1$ sit divisibile.
442. Cum autem tam $b-a$ quam $b+a$ minus sit quam $4q+1$, erit $bb+aa$ per $4q+1$
divisibile. Hinc proposito numero primo $4q+1$, semper summa duorum quadratorum $aa+bb$ per
eum divisibilis exhiberi potest, ita ut neutra radix superet $2q$, et quidem alterum quadratum pro
lubitu assumi potest.
443. Supra autem jam ostendimus summam duorum quadratorum $aa+bb$ inter se primorum,
praeter binarium alios divisores primos non admittere, nisi formae $4n+1$. Unde concludi posse
videtur, omnes numeros primos formae $4q+1$ ipsos esse summas duorum quadratorum, certe autem
vel $2(4q+1)$, vel $5(4q+1)$, vel $13(4q+1)$ etc. erit summa duorum quadratorum.
444. Etsi jam evictum est, plura duobus biquadratis, quorum radices $2q$ non excedant, non
dari, idem residuum relinquentes, tamen hoc etiam seorsim demonstrari potest. Sint enim tres numeri
$a$, $b$, $c$, non excedentes $2q$, ut tam $aa+bb$, quam $aa+cc$ et $bb+cc$ per $4q+1$ essent divisi-
bilia, atque etiam differentiae $aa-cc$, $aa-bb$, $bb-cc$ forent divisibiles. At cum neque $a-c$,
neque $a+c$ per $4q+1$ dividi possit, productum quoque $aa-cc$ dividi non poterit.

methods.what: Elimination showing a product cannot lie in a new class: combine two congruences to derive a contradiction
methods.quote: foret $z(xy - \alpha z) - y(xz - \beta y^\nu)$, hoc est $\beta y^{\nu+1} - \alpha z^2$ quoque divisibile

methods.what: For prime p=4q+1 there are exactly q distinct biquadratic residues, and the non-residues form three classes of q elements each
methods.quote:
si divisor primus fuerit $4q+1$, residua diversa biquadratorum
fore numero $= q$, neque plura, neque pauciora, non-residua autem tribus classibus comprehendi,
quarum quaelibet constet $q$ terminis.

methods.what: Pigeonhole: among the fourth powers of 1..2q, residues coincide in pairs, so b^4 ≡ a^4 mod 4q+1
methods.quote:
dabitur semper alius $b$, et quidem unicus pariter non major quam $2q$, ut $b^4$ et $a^4$ aequalia relinquant
residua, seu ut $b^4 - a^4$ per $4q+1$ sit divisibile.

methods.what: Every prime 4q+1 divides a sum of two squares a^2+b^2 with a,b ≤ 2q, and one square may be chosen arbitrarily
methods.quote:
semper summa duorum quadratorum $aa+bb$ per
eum divisibilis exhiberi potest, ita ut neutra radix superet $2q$, et quidem alterum quadratum pro
lubitu assumi potest.

methods.what: Separate proof that no three fourth powers with roots ≤ 2q share the same residue
methods.quote:
At cum neque $a-c$,
neque $a+c$ per $4q+1$ dividi possit, productum quoque $aa-cc$ dividi non poterit.

videtur, omnes numeros primos formae $4q+1$ ipsos esse summas duorum quadratorum
items.english: Hence it seems that one can conclude that all prime numbers of the form 4q+1 are themselves sums of two squares

items.quote:
certe autem
vel $2(4q+1)$, vel $5(4q+1)$, vel $13(4q+1)$ etc. erit summa duorum quadratorum.
items.english: but certainly either 2(4q+1), or 5(4q+1), or 13(4q+1), etc. will be a sum of two squares.

items.quote: ut § 435 ostendetur, neque $xy$, neque $xz$, neque $yz$ esse posse residuum
items.english: as was shown in § 435, neither xy, nor xz, nor yz can be a residue
